summary: No. Under identical preprocessing, a default RandomForestClassifier reaches a stratified 5-fold CV ROC-AUC of 0.9010, slightly BELOW the 0.9056 of a default LogisticRegression, a difference of -0.0045 AUC. Logistic regression wins in all 5 folds and the paired difference is nominally significant (p=0.0156), so the hypothesis is not supported, though a gap of ~0.005 AUC means the two models are near-equivalent in practice.
primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (RF - LogReg), stratified 5-fold CV mean
methodological_choices: Both estimators used exactly at scikit-learn defaults (only random_state fixed for reproducibility); no tuning, no class_weight, imbalance (23.9% positive) left untouched since ROC-AUC is prevalence-insensitive. Identical preprocessing for both models, fit inside each CV fold via a Pipeline to avoid leakage: numeric columns median-imputed then StandardScaler'd; categorical columns most-frequent-imputed then one-hot encoded (handle_unknown='ignore'). Scaling numerics is a judgement call that matters: it is inert for the forest but without it LogisticRegression's default lbfgs/max_iter=100 fails to converge on capital-gain's 0-99999 range and scores only 0.6373 (which would inflate the gap to +0.2637); I regard the scaled number as the fair baseline. All 14 features kept, including fnlwgt (a census sampling weight, arguably not a legitimate person-level predictor) and race/sex; rows with missing workclass/occupation/native-country were imputed rather than dropped. Validation: StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), shared folds for both models, compared with a paired t-test on the 5 per-fold deltas (n=5 folds, so the p-value is fragile). Sensitivity checks, which show the sign of the result is encoding-dependent and therefore should not be read as a robust 'logistic regression is the better model class': dropping fnlwgt widens the logistic lead (diff -0.0159) and 10x-repeated 5-fold reproduces it (diff -0.0036, RF ahead in only 4/50 folds), but giving the forest ORDINAL-encoded categoricals instead of one-hot lifts it to 0.9059 and erases the gap entirely (diff +0.0003, paired p=0.763) - a tie. So the honest reading is that the two model classes are within ~0.005 AUC of each other and which one 'wins' is decided by preprocessing choices rather than by the model class. Another researcher might reasonably have used ordinal/target encoding for the trees, dropped fnlwgt, added polynomial/interaction terms to the logistic model, or raised max_iter instead of scaling.
